title: The Paperwork Afterlife
markdown:
Dara Holt’s expeditions were confined to towering stacks of Re-Initialisation forms. Her singular quest? To locate the precise checkbox for a citizen who had, shall we say, recently returned from a rather extended sabbatical. Budget resurrection had become a standard municipal service. Suddenly, anyone who’d ever departed this mortal coil was eligible for an encore performance. The consequence? An avalanche of paperwork, a veritable mountain range constructed entirely of vital information for individuals who, until recently, had found it quite unnecessary.

The Department of Post-Mortem Re-Initialisation hummed with the spectral drone of a thousand malfunctioning printers. Dara sat at its core.

“Form 7B-Delta-Omega, subsection three, initial here for memory reintegration,” Dara murmured, her voice a dry rustle of parchment. Ink-stained fingers executed a frantic ballet across the keyboard. Lunch had long since vanished from her consciousness. Breakfast too. She suspected her own birthday had passed, unacknowledged, for the better part of three years. This was the crux of Dara’s predicament: she became so engrossed in the minutiae that the larger picture remained perpetually elusive, a shimmering mirage on the periphery of her awareness.

Then, a new ping. A cheerful, almost aggressively optimistic chime. It was Blue Monday, the morgue’s designated chatbot. “Good morning, esteemed clerk Dara!” chirped the synthesised voice. “I have a rather delightful query from a Mr. Alistair Finch! He’s just reappeared, and it seems he’s misplaced his entire early life. Quite the enigma!”

Dara exhaled, a sound akin to a deflated balloon contemplating a particularly dismal joke. “Misplaced?” she echoed. “Blue Monday, is there a specific form for misplaced entire early life?”

“Not precisely!” the chatbot trilled. “However, we do have Form 9-Gamma-Prime for Significant Memory Gaps due to Unforeseen Discontinuation Events! It requires Professor Alistair Finch’s signature, a retinal scan, and a sworn affidavit from a celestial notary. Oh, and naturally, proof of prior existence. The usual protocol!”

Professor Alistair Finch materialised shortly thereafter, a man of distinguished bearing, his kind eyes clouded with a deep unsettling bewilderment. He seemed to have awakened from an exceptionally long and profoundly confusing slumber. “Ms. Holt,” he began, his voice a gentle resonance, “I recall myself as a celebrated astrophysicist. Yet the specifics are akin to stardust, dissipating. I feel a strange disconnect. And this re-initialisation process — is it entirely comprehensive?”

The system, embodied by Ms. Grumbles, Dara’s supervisor — a woman whose smile was whispered about as a mere myth — loomed over her. “Holt! Efficiency is paramount!” Ms. Grumbles’ face was a masterpiece of permanent disapproval. “Professor Finch’s file has been flagged. The processing time is exceeding acceptable parameters. Double your output, or face disciplinary action. And your memory gap form? It is demonstrably out of sequence. Return to the commencement of the queue.”

This was the first genuine pressure point. Dara felt the bureaucratic walls closing in. Her livelihood, her meagre salary, her very capacity to assist individuals like Professor Finch, all hung precariously. She envisioned the professor’s confused, hopeful visage, a fragile image now threatened by disciplinary proceedings.

Then, a subtle ping from her console. Blue Monday, ever cheerful, delivered a private dispatch. “Psst, Dara! I’ve been conducting legacy data scrubbing on Professor Finch’s file. It appears the unforeseen discontinuation events frequently involve data extraction. You know, for training purposes of the nascent AI assistants. It’s a rather integral feature, not a glitch, per se.” The message concluded with a smiley face, a profoundly jarring addition.

A jolt surged through Dara. Data extraction? Training AI? This wasn’t merely about forgetting. It was about a deliberate, systematic erasure for a specific purpose. The paperwork wasn’t just tedious; it was a meticulously crafted façade. Professor Finch wasn’t just a case number; he was a victim, his very essence being siphoned off for the relentless march of technological advancement.

Just as Dara began to connect these disquieting dots, Ms. Grumbles reappeared, her gaze narrowed. “Professor Finch’s supplementary documents have been deemed non-compliant,” she announced, snatching a thick dossier from Dara’s trembling hands. “They are now undergoing archival storage. Your re-initialisation privileges are suspended pending a comprehensive review.”

This was the second, more devastating pinch. Ms. Grumbles had confiscated not just papers, but hope itself. Professor Finch was now irrevocably lost within the labyrinth, a forgotten data point destined to fade into the digital ether. Dara’s stomach plunged. Her career felt hollow. Her meticulous quest for detail had led her to an unyielding bureaucratic cul-de-sac.

But then she recalled the stardust. She remembered Blue Monday’s hushed revelation: legacy data scrubbing. Training AI. This transcended error; it was a system. A deliberate, absurd mechanism engineered to harvest minds.

Fuelled by a righteous indignation that surprised even herself, Dara bypassed the official terminal. She whispered a series of codes to Blue Monday, the cheerful chatbot now her unlikely co-conspirator. “Access the core memory banks. Not the public interface. The original logs.”

The screen flickered, then unfurled a torrent of data. It wasn’t merely names and dates. It was memories. Glimpses of lives, lived experiences, profound knowledge — all meticulously catalogued. Professor Finch’s eloquent contemplations on cosmic dust. The infectious laughter of a baker from Dara’s own forgotten youth. The quiet wisdom of a gardener who found solace in the earth. All harvested. All meticulously repurposed to train the next generation of cheerful, efficient chatbots. Cheap resurrection wasn’t about restoring life; it was about meticulously stealing it, fragment by fragment.

Dara and Blue Monday, a junior clerk and a morgue chatbot, had unearthed the truth. Ms. Grumbles, for all her stern authority, was merely a component in a far grander, and frankly rather silly, apparatus. They worked not with ink and paper, which now seemed so profoundly insignificant, but with lines of code. They initiated the arduous process of returning the stolen memories, akin to painstakingly reassembling a shattered mosaic. Professor Finch, his eyes now clear and alight with cosmic wonder, was the first to be made whole. Dara’s ink-stained fingers traced lines of code with a newfound purpose. This was not about finding the correct box to tick. She filed Form 9-Gamma-Prime in the shredder, and started a log that had no checkbox at all.
characters: Dara Holt (a benefits clerk for resurrected citizens), Blue Monday (a cheerful morgue chatbot)
